text: Lean 4 for the JavaScript and WebAssembly world. Lasm compiles ordinary Lean 4 programs ahead of time to WebAssembly. One Lean code base can become a Node server, a serverless or edge function, a WASI/Fastly module or a browser app. Because it is Lean, you can prove properties of the code you deploy. The flagship example, Conduit , is the RealWorld app with 117 proved theorems. Lasm ships on npm and brings Lean, Lake and its build tools with it; you only need Node (or Bun or Deno). npm create @lasm@latest my-app -- --template hono # then: cd my-app && npm install && npm run dev AI agents: this README is complete on its own. llms.txt is the short index, and docs/AI.md lists the rules that save you from wrong turns. If Lasm is useful to you, I'd appreciate your sponsorship ( more below ). Every row is tested in CI with the platform's own local runtime, image or emulator. By project policy CI never deploys to a real cloud account ( how each is tested ). Node builds have Lean's full runtime (threads, files, processes, sockets). The edge, Bun/Deno, WASI and browser builds run Lean single-threaded, without sockets or processes (and without files, except on WASI); the rest of Lean works. Every example has a README with a one-command run; examples/README.md lists them all. examples/conduit is Conduit , the RealWorld app (a Medium clone), written entirely in Lean: the REST API, the server-rendered browser app and the proofs. All of this runs in CI ( conduit.yml , run 40615274657, with @lasm/cli 0.3.4). cd examples/conduit npm install # @lasm/cli, Hurl and Playwright (the official suites' runners) npm run build && npm start # http://localhost:3000: the app and its API on Node npm run proofs # check all 117 theorems npm test # the official API suite (also test:workers, test:bun) npx playwright install chromium && npm run test:e2e # the official end-to-end suite npm run build:workers && npx wrangler dev # Cloudflare Workers with local D1 npm run build:bun && npm run start:bun # Bun with bun:sqlite 60-second start A single file needs no project. Save this complete program as Main.lean : def main : IO Unit := do IO.println s! " Hello from Lean! 2 + 3 = {2 + 3} " npx @lasm/cli Main.lean # builds and runs: Hello from Lean! 2 + 3 = 5 npx @lasm/cli build Main.lean # writes dist/; run it with: node dist/main.mjs The first build on a new machine fetches Lean and the build tools once (about 250–275 MB; 19 s for that first build on the Linux CI runner). Later dev builds of a one-line change take about 1–2 s. Each recipe is complete: create, develop, build, deploy. Lasm never installs or starts a platform's own CLI ( wrangler , vercel , fastly , …); you run those. npm run dev is lasm dev : it rebuilds about 2 s after each save and restarts the server, and keeps the last good build running when there is a type error. Node server (Hono; also express , fastify , std-http , fetch ). npm create @lasm@latest my-api -- --template hono cd my-api && npm install npm run dev # http://localhost:3000/hello/Ada npm run build && npm start # dist/ needs only Node 24+ docker build -t my-api . && docker run -p 8080:8080 my-api # the generated Dockerfile AWS Lambda / Vercel / Netlify / Azure / Google Cloud Functions. npm create @lasm@latest my-fn -- --template hono --deploy lambda-zip # or vercel, netlify, azure, gcf, lambda-edge cd my-fn && npm install npm run build:lambda # dist/ and lambda.zip (handler lasm-lambda.handler) # deploy lambda.zip with the AWS console, aws CLI or SAM; recipes: docs/deploy/lambda.md Cloudflare Workers (and Vercel Edge, Netlify Edge, Deno Deploy, Supabase). npm create @lasm@latest my-edge -- --template hono --deploy workers cd my-edge && npm install npm run build:workers # workers/ (wrangler.toml came from lasm init) npx wrangler dev # local workerd; npx wrangler deploy to publish Fastly Compute, WASI, Spin. npm create @lasm@latest my-svc -- --template fetch --deploy fastly --deploy spin cd my-svc && npm install npm run build:fastly && fastly compute serve # Viceroy on http://127.0.0.1:7676 npm run build:wasi-http && spin up # or: wasmtime serve wasi-http/main.wasm Browser app. npm create @lasm@latest my-web -- --template web cd my-web && npm install npm run dev # http://127.0.0.1:5173, live reload npm run build # dist/: a static site for any host or CDN Full stack (server + browser + verified API). npm create @lasm@latest my-app -- --template fullstack cd my-app && npm install npm run dev # one URL: http://127.0.0.1:3000 npm run build && npm start # Node; also build:workers, build:bun, build:deno Editor. Run npx lasm editor once per project; lasm init , lasm dev and lasm build also do it. The Lean editor (VS Code's Lean 4 extension) then resolves import Lasm.* ( details ). The fullstack template is one Lean project with a server ( Lasm.Fetch ), a browser app ( Lasm.UI ) and the API between them ( Lasm.RPC ). The rule a request must satisfy is written and proved once, in Shared.lean , which both sides import ( templates/fullstack ): -- Shared.lean @[irreducible] def checkTitle (title : String) : Except String Unit := let n := (clean title).length if n = 0 then .error " Write something first. " else if n > maxTitle then .error s! " Keep it under {maxTitle} characters. " else .ok () /-- Proved once, holds in the browser and on the server. -/ theorem checkTitle_ok {title : String} (h : checkTitle title = .ok ()) : 0 < (clean title).length ∧ (clean title).length ≤ maxTitle := by unfold checkTitle at h by_cases h0 : (clean title).length = 0 · simp [h0] at h · by_cases h1 : (clean title).length > maxTitle · simp [h0, h1] at h · omega def addTodo : Endpoint NewTodo Todo := { name := " addTodo " , validate := fun r => checkTitle r.title } -- Server.lean: storing a todo demands the proof that its title passed the check, -- and `addTodo.serve` hands the handler that proof (`ok`) after re-validating. def Store.add (s : Store) (title : String) (_ : checkTitle title = .ok ()) : Store × Todo := let t := { id := s.next, title := clean title, done := false } ({ todos := s.todos.push t, next := s.next + 1 }, t) addTodo.serve fun req ok => do let (s, t) := (← load kv).add req.title ok save kv s return .ok t -- Client.lean: a theorem about the browser app: it never sends an invalid title. theorem add_invalid (m : Model) (e : String) (h : checkTitle m.draft = .error e) : (update .add m). 2 .effects = [.msg (.added (.error (.invalid e)))] := addTodo.call_invalid { title := m.draft } Msg.added " " e h Where proofs live and how they are checked. Not proved, tested in CI instead: the JSON/HTTP transport between client and server, the JavaScript that applies patches to the real DOM, the Lasm compiler and runtime, and the browsers. Lean's own compiler is trusted, as in any Lean program ( UI.md , RPC.md ). Declare each JavaScript function you call with one line; the Lean type says how values convert. A complete program (Node's global fetch ): import Lasm.JS open Lasm.JS /-- `await fetch(url, init)` (Node's global fetch) -/ @[js " globalThis " " fetch " ] opaque fetch : String → Data → IO Value def main : IO Unit := do let response ← fetch " https://example.com " (obj []) IO.println s! " {← response.get " status " Nat}: {(← response.callMethodAwait " text " #[] String).length} characters " The rules for writing bindings: Full guide, with Express, Hono, pg , jose and fetch examples and an agent checklist: docs/JS_BINDINGS.md . All numbers are from CI on a free GitHub runner (4-CPU AMD EPYC, Linux x64), candidate 0.1.0-experimental.40494203854 (2026-10-27) unless another run is named. Full tables, method and caveats: BENCHMARKS.md . Lean on Node pays for WebAssembly and its threads. A cold start is CPU-bound, so it grows on small serverless CPU shares, and every JavaScript call crosses threads. Pure-Lean Std.Http on Node is slow (1,290 req/s), so use Hono, Express, Fastify or Lasm.Fetch for production HTTP. Arithmetic on numbers with thousands of digits is slower than native Lean (no GMP). If Lasm is useful to you or you want to see it succeed, I'd appreciate your sponsorship: github.com/sponsors/lastmjs . It supports me and the work on Lasm and the other Millillion projects. My first goal is $250 a month, enough for one dedicated Claude Code account for Lasm. You can also help by starring the repo, trying it, and reporting what breaks . Everything below is the precise contract: every command and option, supported machines and platforms, and exactly what a deployed Lean program cannot do. Install in a project with npm install -D @lasm/cli (the bin is lasm ), or run without installing: npx @lasm/cli Main.lean . npm create @lasm runs lasm init of the same @lasm/cli version with the arguments unchanged. With the Main.lean from the quick start : npx lasm Main.lean # build (dev profile) and run: Hello from Lean! 2 + 3 = 5 npx lasm build Main.lean # write dist/ (release profile) npx lasm --version # version, Lean, runtime and platform (for bug reports) node dist/main.mjs # run the deployment: only Node is needed npx lasm build Main.lean --target lambda # dist/ and an AWS Lambda zip Command or option Example Effect Run (default) npx lasm Main.lean Build (dev profile) and run Lean main . npm run dev in a plain project runs this. Explicit run npx lasm run Main.lean Same as the default command. Run a release build npx lasm Main.lean --release Build and run exactly what lasm build deploys. Program arguments npx lasm Main.lean -- hello "two words" Pass arguments to main (args : List String) . Watch, rebuild, restart (0.3.0) npx lasm dev , npx lasm dev Main.lean --target workers -- arg Watch the Lean sources and the Lake/npm configuration, rebuild after each change (dev profile, one long-lived build worker) and restart the program ( --target node , bun , deno ; default: the runtime running Lasm). A build error is printed with its file, line and source line; the last good program keeps running. Edge targets only rebuild their output directory, which the platform's own local server serves (Lasm never starts platform tools or browsers). --target browser serves the app with live reload ( --port , --host , --no-watch ); several outputs build together: --target node=Server.lean,browser=Client.lean . --release builds the release profile, --no-run only rebuilds, rs + Enter rebuilds and restarts. Details . Build npx lasm build Main.lean Write dist/ (release profile); do not run the application. Dev build npx lasm build Main.lean --dev Write dist/ faster, without the size optimizations. Output directory npx lasm build Main.lean --output "app dist" Choose the deployment directory. lasm build Main.lean "app dist" is an alias. Function platforms npx lasm build Main.lean --target lambda Build dist/ , then package it: node (default; dist/ only), lambda ( lambda.zip ), lambda-edge ( lambda-edge.zip ), vercel ( .vercel/output ), netlify ( netlify/functions/lasm ), azure ( azure-functions/ ), gcf ( gcf/ ). --target=vercel also works. Lasm never installs or starts the platform's CLI. Recipes . Edge isolates (0.2.0) npx lasm build Main.lean --target workers Relink single-threaded with a pure-JS host: workers ( workers/ ), vercel-edge ( api/lasm.mjs , api/_lasm/ ), netlify-edge ( netlify/edge-functions/lasm.mjs , netlify/lasm/ ), deno-deploy ( deno/main.mjs ), supabase-edge ( supabase/functions/<name>/ ; Asyncify, since Supabase's runtime has no JSPI). The edge runtime ships inside @lasm/cli . Guides: Workers , Vercel Edge , Netlify Edge , Deno Deploy , Supabase ; design and limits . Bun and Deno (0.2.0) bunx --bun @lasm/cli Main.lean , deno run -A npm:@lasm/cli Main.lean , bun create @lasm my-app --template hono The compiler runs with Bun or Deno as its only JavaScript runtime and produces the same bytes. Under Bun or Deno the default target is that runtime: --target bun writes bun/main.mjs , --target deno writes deno/main.mjs (portable profile). Deno skips npm versions younger than 24 hours: right after a release, pass --minimum-dependency-age=0 . Bun and Deno . Browser (0.3.0) npx lasm build Main.lean --target browser Write dist/ as a static site: app.<hash>.js (the loader: mount(element, { flags, hydrate }) , auto-mount of <div data-lasm-app> ), app.<hash>.wasm , brotli and gzip copies, app.js , index.html (yours with the loader injected, or a generated page), your public/ files and lasm-manifest.json . --suspend jspi lets blocking waits suspend where the browser has JSPI. --bundler leaves npm imports for a bundler; in Vite: import lasm from '@lasm/cli/vite' , then import app from './Main.lean?lasm' . Web APIs from Lean: import Lasm.Web . Guides: BROWSER.md , UI.md , deploying . WASI, wasi-http, Fastly (0.3.0) npx lasm build Main.lean --target wasi (or wasi-http , fastly ) No JavaScript. wasi writes wasi/main.wasm ( wasi_snapshot_preview1 : wasmtime run --dir . wasi/main.wasm , wasmer, node:wasi ); wasi-http writes wasi-http/main.wasm , a wasi:http/proxy@0.2 component ( wasmtime serve , Spin); fastly writes bin/main.wasm and pkg/<name>.tar.gz ( fastly compute serve / deploy ). No sockets, processes or signals. WASI.md , Fastly . HTTP in pure Lean (0.3.0) import Lasm.Fetch … def main := Lasm.Fetch.serve handle One Request → Async Response handler serves Node ( $HOST:$PORT ), the edge targets, Bun, Deno, Fastly, wasi-http and WASI as CGI; Lasm.Fetch.fetch sends requests; Response.streaming streams. FETCH.md . Force rebuilding npx lasm build Main.lean --rebuild Ignore a cached application build. Detailed diagnostics npx lasm Main.lean --verbose Show compiler and linker details. Help npx lasm --help , npx lasm init --help Show usage; -h is an alias. Version npx lasm --version Print lasm 0.3.5 (@lasm/cli; Lean 4.35.0; Node 26.12.1; linux-x64) ; -v is an alias. New project npm create @lasm@latest my-app -- --template hono or npx @lasm/cli init my-app --template hono Create a Lake project in a new or empty directory ( Main.lean , App.lean , lakefile, lean-toolchain , package.json , README.md , .gitignore , and for servers a Dockerfile and .dockerignore ). Templates: see Start here . --deploy (repeatable) adds a platform's files and npm run build:<target> : lambda ( Dockerfile.lambda , a container image), lambda-zip , lambda-edge , vercel , netlify , azure , gcf ; workers , vercel-edge , netlify-edge , deno-deploy (templates hono , fetch , fullstack ), supabase-edge ( hono ); fastly , wasi-http , spin ( fetch , fullstack ), wasi ( fetch , plain ). The fetch and fullstack templates and their targets are 0.3.0. Writes files only; run npm install next. -t is an alias of --template ; --template=hono also works. Package an existing build npx lasm package --target lambda Package a built server (default dist/ ) for a function platform without rebuilding: the same targets and outputs as lasm build --target , except node . --output PATH chooses the output. Checks the platform's size limit. Refuses a dev build unless --allow-dev . For a browser build, npx lasm package dist --target browser checks every file against lasm-manifest.json and writes _headers . Editor support (0.3.0) npx lasm editor Make the Lean editor (VS Code's Lean 4 extension, any Lean language server client) resolve import Lasm.* in this Lake project: links Lasm's Lean 4.35.0 with its library as the elan toolchain lasm-4.35.0-… and sets it as the directory's elan override ( elan override unset undoes it). lasm init (when Lasm's Lean is already installed), lasm dev and lasm build do the same, printing one line per project, except on CI or with LASM_EDITOR=0 . Editor setup . Cache repair npx lasm cache repair Offline verification and removal of invalid tools and abandoned staging. Refuses an active build. --rebuild and --verbose work with run and build. --output and --target are build-only; arguments after -- are run-only. The application's exit status is preserved. npx lasm --version ( -v ) prints the version, Lean release, JavaScript runtime and platform (include it in bug reports). There is no install, clean or uninstall subcommand. Build profiles. Both link the same program with the same libraries and are deterministic. release ( lasm build , lasm Main.lean --release ): the full Binaryen size optimization; byte-reproducible; the one to deploy. dev ( lasm Main.lean , lasm dev , lasm build --dev ): leaves those passes out and compiles your modules at -O1 ; it behaves the same, builds several seconds faster, and its program.wasm is about 15–20 % larger. A dev rebuild starts from the project's previous build, so its bytes can depend on that build. build-info.json records "profile" . lasm package and lasm build --dev --target <platform> refuse a dev build unless you pass --allow-dev . Environment variables (all optional): Other LASM_* variables in the source are maintainer diagnostics, not a supported interface. Installation. npm install @lasm/cli brings Lean and the build tools as exact-pinned @lasm/… npm packages for your platform through your own registry, proxy and cache. The Lake/ Lean -import data and, only for Lake projects with C code, the C tier ( @lasm/lean-c-<platform> ) are fetched with your npm on first use. The terminal shows progress; later builds reuse verified tools and unchanged outputs. On a new machine, without the download, a first Hono build took 25.7 s (Linux x64), 27.8 s (Linux arm64), 44.4 s (Windows), 58.7 s (Apple Silicon) and 141.9 s (Intel Mac) on the CI runners ( build time , run 40131930601). Cache locations and recovery: NODE_SUPPORT.md , INSTALLATION_HARDENING.md . Git is needed only for Lake projects with Git or Reservoir dependencies; Lasm uses the git on your PATH and says how to install it when it is missing. Existing Lake projects build with npx lasm build Main.lean from the project directory. Pin leanprover/lean4:v4.35.0 in lean-toolchain ; other versions are rejected with Unsupported Lean toolchain … Lasm supports Lean v4.35.0 . A per-package compatibility list covers Batteries, Cli, LSpec, Plausible, Aesop, Qq, leansqlite, UnicodeBasic, MD4Lean, lean-zip, lean4-parser, lean-redis and others; packages not on it are untested. Machines that build with Lasm (the compiler): Node 24 or newer (tested: 24.0.0, 24.22.1, 26.12.1). No engine flags. Exact tested artifacts: NODE_ACCEPTANCE.md . A Node dist/ needs Node 24 or newer (Node 22 and older stop with This application requires Node 24.0.0 or newer ) and at least 512 MB of memory . It runs on Linux x64 and arm64 (glibc 2.28+, or musl/Alpine) from a build on any supported platform, and on the build machine's own platform. Copy all of dist/ ; no Lean source, npm install or build tools are needed there. Each platform below is tested in CI with the local runtime, image or emulator named; none with a real cloud account. Full matrix: DEPLOYMENT.md . A dist/ built on Windows and copied to Linux other than through docker build needs chmod 755 dist/host/native/process/linux-* . Node's --jitless cannot work (it disables WebAssembly). Hosts that cap virtual memory ( ulimit -v , vm.overcommit_memory=2 ) refuse the Node build, which reserves about 22 GB of address space. Node 26's official binary needs libatomic1 on minimal images that install the tarball themselves. Builds enforce ahead-of-time execution. Ordinary functions, recursion, closures, inductive types, pattern matching, type classes, dependent types and compiled IO are supported. Imports, macros, elaboration, tactics, deriving, proofs and #eval run during compilation in managed native Lean. Initializers count as runtime dependencies: a broad import Lean can retain the compiler; use meta import Lean when only macros or tactics need it, and narrower imports for runtime data libraries ( import Lean with Lean.Json , and deriving ToJson, FromJson , build and run). Each rejection is explained: Lasm prints the chain from your code to the compiler code and, when a broad import is the cause, the narrower modules your code uses. Deployed programs honor LEAN_ABORT_ON_NONLINEAR=1 as native Lean does. Per-platform results: language coverage . The deployed application cannot use: The build checks reachable runtime dependencies , including imported libraries and indirect calls; a reachable forbidden call is rejected even if your input would not take that branch, and dead code removed by the linker does not count. The launcher also rejects missing, stale or incompatible capability records before loading the application (a consistency check, not a security sandbox). There is no large compatibility fallback. Lake packages. Modules imported only for compilation (tactics, elaborators, for example Aesop, Qq or import Lean for macros) do not keep Lean's compiler in the deployment. Lasm runs a module's initializers only when the program uses something they define or register, or when they are the program's own code doing IO or calling C ( --verbose shows how many were skipped). C source that a package bundles ( extern_lib , moreLinkObjs , for example leansqlite's SQLite) is compiled with Lean's own clang, fetched once as the C tier (39–52 MB); no system C compiler is needed (macOS needs the Xcode Command Line Tools SDK for C library headers). Prebuilt native libraries (shared libraries, -l options: libcurl, OpenSSL, libpq, BLAS) cannot be linked; the build names the library and the package. Not release guarantees. Console output, arguments, exit codes, local Lake imports and selected language/filesystem fixtures have native-versus-Node tests, and before 0.1.0 Lean's runtime-capable upstream suite and 19 ecosystem projects ran on all five platforms with zero regressions against the previous accepted candidate ( 0.1.0 gate ). Complete IO.FS , concurrency, subprocess/signal/terminal parity, every third-party library and the full upstream suite are not guaranteed ( IO gaps ). Big numbers ( Nat / Int beyond 63 bits) use Lean's own arbitrary-precision code instead of GNU MP, so apps contain no LGPL code; results equal native Lean's, but at 10,000 digits multiplication is about 5× and Nat.gcd about 60× slower than with GMP in Wasm ( numbers ). Lake dependencies use your system Git ( system Git ). 0.1.0 was the first npm release ( notes ); 0.2.0 adds edge targets and Bun/Deno ( notes ); 0.3.0 adds the browser, Lasm.UI , full-stack apps, WASI/Fastly and the editor support ( notes ); 0.3.1 puts the starter code under MIT-0 and adds bug-report pointers ( notes ); 0.3.2 fixes Std.Internal.UV sockets, timers and signals ( notes ); 0.3.3 was never published, and its changes shipped in 0.3.4 ( notes ); 0.3.5 updates the README and the Conduit example ( notes ). Lasm's npm packages ( @lasm/cli , @lasm/create and the @lasm/… tool packages) are published only by the release.yml workflow, through npm trusted publishing with provenance: no npm tokens exist. A release is a pull request that bumps the package.json version and is published only after the release-checks status (five-platform candidate checks; edge, Bun/Deno, browser, Lasm.UI, WASI/Fastly, fullstack, unit and dev-loop checks; and an npm rehearsal of the exact packages) passed for the released commit. Found a bug? npx lasm --version gives the version line the bug report form asks for. npm view @lasm/cli@<version> shows the provenance, and npm audit signatures in a project verifies it.
